cotcny-2ea8GwCOmR4xUZzuuc2AR9: This Sunday, Pastor Jon continued A Manifesto of Fruitfulness, teaching from Galatians 5:13–26 on the fruit of the Spirit. The fruit of the Spirit isn't something we manufacture by trying harder. It is the evidence of a life being transformed by Christ. Fruit comes through union, not imitation; by beholding, not striving; in community, not isolation. As we remain planted in Him, the Spirit slowly forms us into people who reflect the character of Jesus.
cotcny-1YGYwCGaqbnZQbVWkas4FF: This Sunday, Pastor Jon continued our series, A Manifesto of Fruitfulness, teaching from Luke 8:4-15, the parable of the sower. Pastor Jon reminded us that Jesus describes one seed, scattered generously across every kind of ground. The variance wasn't the seed, but the soil. He named the four kinds soil could take: seed stolen before it can root, joy that springs up fast and withers under real pressure, a heart slowly choked by the decade-long apartment search, the co-op board interview, a city built to manufacture not-enough, until there's no margin left to notice God, and soil that receives the word, keeps it, and yields a hundred times what was sown, a harvest so disproportionate to the effort that it can only be received as gift. Jon closed with an invitation: not a program to complete, but a simple surrender of the soil itself. Lord, make us good soil.
cotcny-4t3D72K7iKl2IQtaEFuro1: This Sunday, Pastor Jon returned from sabbatical and opened a new series called, A Manifesto of Fruitfulness, starting with Jesus's words in John 15: "Abide in me." He named some of the places we try to root our lives instead: self-preservation, achievement, religious performance, and the quiet exhaustion each one leaves behind, especially in a city that trains us to keep building, proving, becoming. But Jesus offers a different picture entirely: a branch doesn't strain to produce fruit, it simply stays connected to the vine, and the fruit follows on its own. Pastor Jon called this his life ambition—becoming, in his words, a "black belt in abiding"—learning to receive the love of Jesus rather than spend a lifetime trying to earn it. The invitation this week is that simple: stop building your life around what you can do for Jesus, and start receiving what he has already done for you.
cotcny-5MAfqq0F7FxtIma1hgE8sW: This Sunday, Pastor Billy closed our FOLLOW series by asking what it would look like to take Jesus' command to go and make disciples seriously—not as a monumental assignment reserved for pastors or people who have it all together, but as an ordinary part of following Jesus. God's discipleship plan is "you!" Pastor Billy said. You already have relationships, access, and places of influence no pastor could replicate. The invitation is to make yourself known as a Christian, ask God for one person to disciple, and look for opportunities to lean in. We do not change heart, Jesus does. Our part is to be faithful with the person He has already placed in front of us.
cotcny-2ZUCshgERUTSG9C9I5HGF5: This Sunday, Pastor Reagan continued our FOLLOW series with a teaching on worship. She began with the story of a woman who poured an entire jar of expensive perfume over Jesus. Where the disciples saw waste; Jesus saw worship. But the question beneath the story is not simply what we are willing to give Jesus, it is what we believe He is worth. Pastor Reagan traced worship back to the act of beholding—to giving our attention to Jesus long enough for our vision of Him to be enlarged. Mary's extravagant offering was not an isolated moment of devotion. It was the natural response of a life that had come to see Jesus as worthy, and when Jesus becomes our highest good, our lives begin to reorder around Him.
cotcny-4jGzo3cyckZ11Hq31vg4XO: This Sunday, Pastor Tim continued our FOLLOW series with Jesus' difficult words to the Pharisees in Matthew 23. Rather than using the passage to confront everyone else, he invited us to ask a more personal question: Where does Jesus want to confront me? Pastor Tim explored how hypocrisy can take root when our outward lives become disconnected from what is happening within us, and how easily we can notice the failures of others while overlooking our own. Jesus' confrontation is not meant to leave us in shame, rather it is an invitation into honesty, mercy, and freedom. Allowig God to form in us what we cannot produce on our own.
cotcny-5CpZudvOnUkhk2di0BlGaO: This week Pastor Keithen continued our Follow series in Matthew 20:25-28, where Jesus tells His disciples that greatness in the kingdom looks nothing like greatness in the world. Preaching to a room full of New Yorkers, Pastor Keithen named the "main character energy" that drives so much of this city, the ambition and grit that gets us here and keeps us here, and asked whether we've quietly assumed Jesus only wants to tweak that energy rather than replace it. He walked through four shifts from the text: from consumption to contribution, from criticism to compassion, from main character energy to a life of consecration, and from extracting from New York to laying our lives down for it. cotcny-6QCbIlGVPDduQKcySpq33f: This Sunday, Pastor Tim continued our FOLLOW series by asking what it means to love God with our whole lives. Pastor Tim reflected on how our love for God is formed through both joy and disappointment, and how faithfulness becomes deeper when we learn to trust His character even when we don't understand His circumstances. That love eventually moves outward, shaping the way we see and love the people God has placed around us. Following Jesus means learning to love God like this, and letting that love change the way we live in the world.
cotcny-6ScZU5a50r3kkL6FMW2sXW: This Sunday, Pastor Ralph continued our FOLLOW series with a teaching on Jesus' invitation to true rest from Matthew 11:25–12:21 He began with John the Baptist, sitting in prison and asking Jesus, "Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?" Rather than promising an easier life, He invites us into a different way of living—one where we come to Him, take His yoke, and learn His way. The result isn't the absence of difficulty, but the deep rest that comes from walking closely with the gentle and humble King.
cotcny-3ZXFazC4TecBIBvzIwIN56: This Sunday, Dr. Ron Walborn continued our Follow series with a teaching on healing from Matthew 8:1–4. He began with the character of Jesus. cotcny-1Rmw38KLUTcqzRPa4lDgFj: This Sunday, guest preacher Dr. Wanda Walborn continued our FOLLOW series with a teaching on obedience from Matthew 7:21-27. The difference was the foundation, quietly formed long before the rain, built with integrity, consistent sowing, and grit. The habits formed in the calm show up in the storm. cotcny-0gK3soz7WX1Z2d2oIKab3e: This week, Pastor Ralph continued our FOLLOW series with a teaching on Jesus' command to "seek first the kingdom of God." cotcny-3WJs56MllxSZfOXircoIou: This week, Pastor Raegan continued our FOLLOW series by teaching from Jesus' temptation in the wilderness in Matt. 4:1–11. cotcny-1WAnqO2rywvXzt1DphDa5I: This week, Pastor Keithen opened our FOLLOW series with a question that kicks off the heart of the series, "Is it possible to be a Christian and not a disciple of Jesus?" cotcny-7q97rzafF9aGyNzExUqUFj: This week, Pastor Jon preached from John 7:53–8:11, using the story of the woman caught in adultery and dragged into the temple courts before a crowd with stones as his text for the freedom Jesus offers us from shame. cotcny-5STgr5mZH8ul69YelC355j: This week, Pastor Ralph Castillo continued the FREED series with a teaching on freedom from idolatry. cotcny-1jcNUpef2Hn4HQmDep8VPz: This Sunday, Pastor Tim continued our FREED series with a teaching on freedom from lies, drawing from John 8:31–47. Pastor Tim argued that the problem is not that we haven't tried hard enough. It's that beneath every sin pattern is a lie we have been carrying so long it feels inseparable from who we are, and no amount of effort will ever reach it. He comes to replace it with something stronger: Himself, the truth that became a person, who walks up to the lie that has been running your life and extinguishes it. cotcny-4362x7iDGGKI55of567iQf: This Sunday, Pastor Sam continued our FREED series with a teaching on freedom from sin, drawing from 1 John 1:5–10, 2:1–2. Through the lens of both guilt-innocence and honor-shame frameworks, Pastor Sam showed that Jesus doesn't just declare us innocent; He restores the relationship. Through the practice of honest, specific, and confident confession, we can walk out of the shadows and into the freedom that is already our inheritance in Christ.
cotcny-0h3pF4HudoMQ3msXhWK8f7: This Sunday, Pastor Jon continued the FREED series with one of the most personal questions it will raise: can you actually be free from your past? He opened with a number—nine out of ten—his and Christy's combined score on the Adverse Childhood Experiences assessment. The score wasn't shared for sympathy, it was shared to make the question real. As James Baldwin wrote, "people are trapped in history, and history is trapped in them." Sin works the same way. It exerts power by keeping you in what has already happened, but the antidote isn't denial. Pastor Jon called the answer, "eschatological realism" — a clear, inhabitable sense of the future God has for you. When you're living from that future, what the present holds over you loses its grip. Paul is the guide. In Philippians 3, a man with a past that could have defined him entirely writes about forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead. Biblical forgetting isn't numbing, rather it's the intentional release of failure, guilt, and the pride that can calcify even around our wounds. In Christ, we've been given an identity more defining than anything we've been through. Scripture gives us a redemptive orientation toward time: a past that has been redeemed, a present marked by wonder, and a future held open by hope.
cotcny-4Q9OIdUpV0zIRB60VLwCEk: This Sunday, Pastor Jon opened the new series "FREED" by putting our cultural moment under pressure. We are the freest people in history, and among the most anxious. The freedom we've been promised has not delivered the peace it advertised. What we got instead was exhaustion, comparison, and a quiet sense of fragmentation. The Bible's definition of freedom is entirely different. The question is not whether you're free to do whatever you want. It's whether you're free to become who you were made to be. Paul, writing to the Galatians, doesn't treat freedom as a footnote to the Gospel, he puts it at the center. From there, Pastor Jon traced what Christ sets us free from: condemnation, religious performance, the pull toward lawlessness, and what we're freed into: a new identity as sons and daughters, the Spirit, a community where we actually belong. Freedom, in this reading, has a direction and a destination. The invitation of this series is honest work: name what has you bound, reject the lies that sustain it, receive the grace of Jesus, and learn to walk in step with the Spirit alongside people telling the truth.
cotcny-1I1VNTJ1zxsE90VskIZFAg: This Resurrection Sunday, Pastor Jon asked a question most of us don't say out loud: what happens to hope when it dies? The disciples on the road to Emmaus knew that feeling. They had built everything around Jesus, and then watched Him die. Walking away from Jerusalem, they said the most honest thing in the passage, "we had hoped..." Into that exact moment, Jesus shows up, not to people with their lives together, but to two people walking in the wrong direction. His next move of opening the Scriptures, sitting down at the table, breaking bread is less a lesson in theology, than an invitation back to life. All the information in the world doesn't close that gap. What changes everything is relationship with the risen Savior.
cotcny-7ACS8CkAUuzDldMF0qRvS7: This Sunday, Pastor Jon concluded the "Come to Me" series by asking a question worth sitting with: why Jesus? He challenged us with the idea of "miswanting": the gap between what we think will satisfy us and what actually does, and made the case that Jesus doesn't shame us for our desires, but wants to save us from the lesser loves we've been chasing. Jesus's invitation in Matthew 11 is not to a system or a philosophy. it's to a person. One you come to, and keep coming to.
cotcny-1ONk9pEjaW2iAcZSg0Ql7O: This Sunday, Pastor Keithen taught from John 11 and made the case that most of us, have gotten the story badly wrong. Not one was about Jesus. From there, he traced the two answers to eternity we've inherited — secularism, which says death is just the end, and a kind of religious gnosticism, which says the physical world is bad and the goal of faith is to escape it. Pastor Keithen argued that neither is what Jesus actually taught. In John 11, standing outside the tomb of his dead friend Lazarus, Jesus doesn't offer Martha a better destination. He weeps. He raises Lazarus bodily from the dead. And before he does, he says the most staggering thing anyone in that world had ever heard: I am the resurrection and the life. He wasn't pointing her toward a place she'd go one day. He was telling her the hope she'd been waiting for was standing right in front of her. Our eternal destiny isn't something transactional, it's relational. And because resurrection is true, it changes how we live right now, not just what happens after.
cotcny-3dVXvxmXS3QGVRP2cwbpcH: This week, Pastor Tim Brown unpacks one of Jesus' most profound declarations — Jesus is the Way, the Truth, and the Life — and gets to the heart of what it means to follow Him. It's a relationship, and there's a sobering difference between knowing about God and truly knowing Him. If you want to know what God is truly like, look at Jesus. His weeping at the tomb of His friend, His washing a betrayer's feet, His forgiving the condemned. He is a compassionate Father worth following, and worth knowing. Pastor Tim concluded with the most invitation to follow Jesus. In Him is life.
cotcny-3nlnvmKniIImXnRFUCwgkm: This week Pastor Jon taught from John 10:11-21, where Jesus declares "I am the good shepherd" and asked a question that cuts straight to the heart of modern life: who is actually forming you? Jesus differentiates Himself from these poor leaders, and proves to be the ultimate Good Shepherd. He is the shepherd who laid His life down by choice His sheep. Pastor Jon encouraged us to choose wisely who shepherds us, and invited us to Christ's abundant path.
cotcny-02YuVxvuyB6Uc3Xg0lvmaS: This Sunday, Pastor Jon taught from John 10:1–10, where Jesus declares "I am the door," and meets us in one of our most quietly carried human aches -- our desire to belong. His door is open to anyone, and through His door isn't merely entry, but protection, freedom, and abundance.

vintage-sm-5UhdNsthhVlsICuGILzt25: Pastor Ger explores what it means to share the love of Jesus in a way that is authentic, relational, and rooted in grace. Through Genesis 12 and stories from the life of Jesus, Ger reminds us that we are blessed to be a blessing—and that evangelism doesn’t have to be complicated or intimidating. Instead, we can create safe spaces for people to explore faith, live with compelling curiosity, love people well, and simply play our part while trusting God with the rest. This message offers a fresh vision for sharing our faith, inviting us to reflect the love of Jesus and help others discover Him for themselves.
vintage-sm-4Hny8xADlWZCabDqXwEVOx: Pastor Ger Jones invites us to explore one of life’s biggest questions: Who is Jesus? Through the story of Nathaniel in John 1 and his own journey from skepticism to faith, Pastor Ger explores what it means to honestly investigate Jesus, wrestle with doubt, and ask the questions that matter most. From searching for meaning in career, success, and pleasure to discovering the love and life found in Jesus, this message is an invitation to come and see for yourself. You don’t have to take a blind leap of faith—you can explore Jesus, ask the hard questions, and discover who He really is.
vintage-sm-4WlayLOxtkG0uaTh4mkYpx: Pastor Kristen Maynard delivers an insightful teaching on Revelation 2, focusing on the church in Ephesus and the critical call to return to "the love you had at first". This message serves as a powerful reminder to prioritize intimacy with God above mere outward performance, encouraging a season of reflection and renewed passion in our walk with Him.
vintage-sm-5hFTPHqGjCT7Nv1PaboULs: Pastor Ger continues our series in Acts, looking at the early church and what it means to be the family of God. vintage-sm-6LzpVjezUHWTqEIXPHi0Nt: Pastor Ger Jones continues our series in Acts as we look at the birth of the early church and the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. vintage-sm-0dtWKawjMhp3wHTbQQ51nr: Pastor Ger Jones kicks off our new series in Acts, inviting us to step into the story of the early church and discover what happens when ordinary people are empowered by the Holy Spirit. vintage-sm-4maQTmDNEMDr4tbO5Aq6JZ: Guest speaker Dr. Esau McCaulley joins us at our Santa Monica location for a powerful message from Jonah, inviting us to consider what it looks like to follow God even when it's difficult.
